playlist.name: Pink Floyd Essentials
playlist.description: Some bands turn into shorthand for a certain sound or style, and Pink Floyd belongs among that elite group. The very name connotes something specific: an elastic, echoing, mind-bending sound that evokes the chasms of space. Pink Floyd grounded that limitless sound with exacting explorations of mundane matters of ego, mind, memory and heart, touching upon madness, alienation, narcissism and society on their concept albums of the 1970s. Of these concept records, ‘Dark Side of the Moon’ resonated strongest, earning new audiences year after year, decade after decade, and its longevity makes sense. That 1973 album distilled the wild psychedelia of their early years — that brief, heady period when they were fronted by Syd Barrett — into a slow, sculpted, widescreen epic masterminded by Roger Waters, the bassist who was the band’s de facto leader in the ’70s. Waters fueled Pink Floyd’s golden years, conceiving such epics as ‘Wish You Were Here’ and ‘The Wall,’ but the band survived his departure in the ’80s, with guitarist David Gilmour stepping to the forefront on ‘A Momentary Lapse of Reason’ and ‘The Division Bell.’ Throughout the years, drummer Nick Mason and keyboardist Rick Wright appeared in some capacity, and the group’s sonic signature was always evident: a wide, expansive sound that was instantly recognizable as their own, yet was adopted by all manner of bands, from guitar-worshiping metalheads to freaky, hippie, ambient electronic duos. Unlike almost any of their peers, Pink Floyd played to both sides of the aisle: They were rooted in the blues, but their heart belonged to the future, a dichotomy that made them a quintessentially modern 20th-century band. (Photo and bio: Rovi)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Live Essentials
playlist.description: No, we can’t bring the Floyd’s out-of-body, surrealist stage show into your living room — the flying pig simply won’t fit — but we can deliver these staples of the live set in the highest sound quality. (Photo: Hipgnosis, Pink Floyd Music Ltd./Press)

playlist.name: Tracks & Traces: Pink Floyd
playlist.description: Pink Floyd is one of the most influential bands in rock history, with a sprawling legacy traversing eras and genres. In this playlist we unfold the story of Pink Floyd as a keystone of popular-music influence, covering the music that inspired them, then tracing their journey through generations of impact. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Evolution: Psychedelic Explorers
playlist.description: This playlist covers the Floyd’s most brazenly psychedelic years of the late ’60s and early ’70s — from their landmark recordings featuring the legendary Syd Barrett through their developing blend of prog-rock storytelling, otherworldly sonics and the smart guitar heroism of David Gilmour. (Cover: Pink Floyd in 1967 / Photo: Andrew Whittuck/Redferns)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Evolution: The Gilmour Years
Pink Floyd Evolution: The Gilmour Years
playlist.description: This playlist traverses the Floyd’s output after the departure of Roger Waters, when David Gilmour led the group through underrated studio recordings and astounding live shows that carried the torch for the group’s blockbuster era. (Cover: Pink Floyd in 1987 / Photo: Ross Marino/Getty Images)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Evolution: Prog-Rock Giants
playlist.description: This playlist features the Floyd as prog auteurs, elevating the rock album to new levels of cultural importance and selling patient, surreal music about madness and the travesties of humanity in numbers great enough to bolster the entire recording industry. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Turn On, Tune In, Drop Out: Psychedelic Classics
Turn On, Tune In, Drop Out: Psychedelic Classics
playlist.description: Inspired by mind altering drugs and the counter culture, the sound of Psychedelic music bloomed out of 1960s California and into the mainstream popular culture, soon affecting most musical styles from funk to folk and spread across the globe. This colorful playlist of psychedelic classics aims to grasp the essence and the breadth of not only a musical direction, but a human state of mind. (Cover: Raimond Klavins, Unsplash).

playlist.description: Immortalized by The Beatles, the legendary Abbey Road Studios has also housed artists like The Hollies, Pink Floyd, Oasis and Radiohead. Since being founded in 1931, the London recording studio is rightfully considered a landmark for 20th century music. (Photo: UMG/press)

playlist.name: Bardo Pond Essentials
playlist.description: Philadelphia’s very own psychedelic mainstays Bardo Pond have been relentlessly dropping music since the early 1990s, and gained reputation as one of the most mind-altering bands out there. Way out there that is, Bard Pond is known for their broad musical approach, embracing space, acid, noise and post-rock, free music, avant-garde and jazz over 20 odd albums and counting. There are no limits or boundaries in their world, and this playlist gives you just a glimpse of cosmic paradise. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.description: The end of an era, and the beginning of a new: Following the aftermath of punk and disco, 1979 marks the rise of electro pioneers and synth-pop and the early days of hip-hop. Massive albums by The Clash (‘London Calling’), Pink Floyd (‘The Wall’) and Michael Jackson (‘Off the Wall’) saw the light of the day, as well as early albums from The Police, Prince, and The Cure. And did music videos killed the radio stars? Find deep album cuts, forgotten gems and the biggest hit singles on this playlist with songs from 1979. [This list of yearly songs follows the rule of earliest release date.] (Cover: Joy Division - Unknown Pleasure, Warner)

playlist.name: David Gilmour Essentials
playlist.description: In Pink Floyd in the mid-’70s, David Gilmour earned a reputation as perhaps the most cinematic of the rock era’s guitar gods. The language of his playing was based in the blues, but his tremendous sound was spectral rather than gloating, and his solos unspooled like melodramas. In many ways, his playing reflected the strange duality of ’70s Floyd on the whole: It was both the stuff of mega-selling classic rock and morose art music. He’d joined the Floyd in 1967, to pick up the slack caused by his schoolmate Syd Barrett’s mental illness, which often manifested onstage. As a songwriter, vocalist and guitarist in collaboration with Roger Waters, he redefined the sonic and conceptual ambition of the rock LP, but the band fractured when Waters’ oversight came to define Pink Floyd’s vision. Gilmour was able to reform the group under his leadership (and sans Waters), shepherding them through an underrated final chapter. Throughout his career, sometimes as an escape from frustrations within his iconic band, Gilmour recorded as a solo artist. This playlist features highlights from those albums. (Photo: Anton Corbijn, Sony/press)

playlist.name: Roger Waters Essentials
playlist.description: George Roger Waters (b. 1943) came to fame as a member of Pink Floyd. Waters experienced every kind of success with the band, and then managed a very successful solo career. He’s hit a commercial peak in recent years touring his stage show of Pink Floyd’s The Wall, called “one of the most ambitious and complex rock shows ever staged.” This list covers Waters’ career highlights as a solo artist. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Space Rock Classics
playlist.description: Few things have fascinated us earthly humans as much as outer space. In the boundless world of music, the cosmos have been a constant source of inspiration for artists searching beyond the scope of their reachable surroundings. From the hopeful futurists of the 1950s (via odes to the lunar landing), to the stadium rock of the 1970s (when the earth became too small for some) to more modern explorers. Here are artists  and songs who in different ways are gazing past the atmosphere, into the vastness of the last frontier. (Photo: Unsplash)

playlist.name: Syd Barrett Essentials
playlist.description: Syd Barrett was one of rock history’s most mysterious, and beloved, tragic geniuses. Founding Pink Floyd in the mid-’60s, Barrett was hugely responsible for the development of their sound, acting as principal songwriter for the band’s 1967 debut, ‘The Piper at the Gates of Dawn,’ a psychedelic masterpiece. Though his talents were unquestionable, Barrett’s fragile mental health and complete immersion into hallucinogenic drugs led him to distance himself from the world, and from the professionalism required to be a bandleader. His solo career was short. ‘The Madcap Laughs’ and ‘Barrett’ were both released in 1970, with help from members of Pink Floyd and the Soft Machine. Though not overwhelmingly successful in commercial terms, both are considered stylistically and technically influential works. In 1972 Barrett gave up music to focus on his family and mental health, living in self-imposed exile until his death in 2006. Perhaps his most loving eulogy comes from the song his former bandmates wrote for him in 1975: “Remember when you were young, you shone like the sun/Now there’s that look in your eyes, like black holes in the sky/Shine on you crazy diamond…” (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Shine On: A Tribute to Syd Barrett
Shine On: A Tribute to Syd Barrett
playlist.description: “Remember when you were young,” sang Roger Waters. “You shone like the sun.” Those near-mythic opening lines of Pink Floyd’s monumental nine-part composition “Shine on You Crazy Diamond,” off the band’s ninth studio album, ‘Wish You Were Here’ (1975), famously refer to Syd Barrett, born Roger Keith Barrett in 1946 in Cambridge, England. In 1965 he formed Pink Floyd, arguably rock’s most important progressive and psychedelic group. Barrett wrote most of the band’s landmark debut album, ‘The Piper at the Gates of Dawn,’ and appeared on its follow-up, ‘A Saucerful of Secrets,’ but left the group before the album was completed due to his declining mental health. He went on to record two acclaimed solo albums, ‘The Madcap Laughs’ and ‘Barrett’ (both 1970), but in 1972 he left the music industry entirely, retired from public life and remained private until his death in 2006. Though active for less than a decade, Syd Barrett built a legacy that has only grown throughout the years, with artists such as David Bowie, Wayne Coyne and Robyn Hitchcock citing him as an essential influence. This playlist collects both cover versions and tribute songs from Barrett’s old bandmates and such artists as Daniel Treacy, the Brian Jonestown Massacre and Paul Weller.
